props.title: The Chinese Parrot

sections.content: **The Chinese Parrot (1927)** (1927) represents a crucial early Hollywood adaptation of Earl Derr Biggers' Charlie Chan novels, marking the second film appearance of the Asian detective. While considered lost today, this Universal production starred Japanese actor Kamiyama Sojin as Chan, following George Kuwa's debut in The House Without a Key (1926). The film's significance extends beyond its detective story elements - it captures Hollywood's complex relationship with Asian representation during the silent era, preceding the more famous Warner Oland and Sidney Toler interpretations of Chan in the 1930s and 40s. sections.content: The lost status of **The Chinese Parrot** (1927) makes it particularly intriguing for film historians studying the evolution of Asian characters in American cinema. Director Paul Leni, fresh from his success with The Cat and the Canary (1927), brought his German Expressionist style to this mystery, likely influencing later Chan films. The production marked one of the few instances where an Asian actor portrayed Chan before the role became associated with white actors in yellowface.

The film's plot, following Chan's investigation of a pearl necklace transaction, reflected common mystery tropes of the era seen in films like **The Bat** (1926) and **London After Midnight** (1927). However, its treatment of the Chan character differed significantly from later interpretations, with Sojin's portrayal reportedly more serious and less reliant on the broken English and aphorisms that would become series staples. sections.content: The casting of Kamiyama Sojin represented a rare moment of authentic Asian representation in 1920s Hollywood, contrasting with contemporaneous yellowface performances like Lon Chaney in **Mr. Wu** (1927) and Richard Barthelmess in **Broken Blossoms** (1919). This casting choice becomes even more significant considering the subsequent decades of white actors portraying Chan, starting with Warner Oland in **Charlie Chan Carries On** (1931).
